claims.text: The magnitude of local lattice distortion is the dominant factor governing yield strength and deformation behavior in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Atomic size differences give rise to local lattice distortion.
Composition can be altered to vary the atomic-size-mismatch delta parameter.
Greater atomic size mismatch produces greater local lattice distortion.
The proposed comparison holds grain size, precipitate distributions, and processing conditions constant while varying atomic size mismatch.
The mechanical comparison is to be conducted by room-temperature tensile testing at a fixed strain rate.
Electron microscopy can be used to verify comparable grain size and precipitate structure.
Local lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
Greater lattice distortion pins dislocations more effectively during deformation.
Dislocations move more easily in an alloy with lower atomic size mismatch.
More effective impediment of dislocation motion increases yield strength.
More effective impediment of dislocation motion alters work-hardening behavior.
The higher-distortion alloy is predicted to have greater yield strength than the lower-mismatch baseline.
The higher-distortion alloy is predicted to have modified work-hardening characteristics relative to the baseline.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold when grain size, precipitates, processing conditions, test temperature, and strain rate are controlled.
Short-range chemical ordering and minor precipitate effects may also contribute to strength and deformation behavior.
The hypothesis would be falsified if greater predicted lattice distortion produced no statistically significant yield-strength increase and no altered dislocation behavior relative to the baseline.
